5 Nonlinear Interactions

Much of what makes network analysis interesting is how ramifications of choices flow across networks. In general, decisions made at a given node iii affect responses of neighboring nodes and, through them, neighbors of neighboring nodes, and so on. As these consequences flow across the network, they in turn affect choices at iii. This is a tail-chasing scenario, which can be unraveled through fixed point theory.

In some network settings, such as the input-output model in Section 2.1, interactions are linear and fixed point problems reduce a system of linear equations. In other settings, interactions are inherently nonlinear and, as a result, we need more sophisticated fixed point theory.

This chapter is dedicated to the study of networks with nonlinear interactions. We begin with relevant fixed point theory and then apply it to a sequence of problems that arise in analysis of economic networks, including production models with supply constraints and financial networks.

5.1Fixed Point Theory¶

Let SSS be any set. Recall from Section 6.1.1.6 that, given a self-map GGG on SSS, a point x∈Sx \in Sx∈S is called a fixed point of GGG if Gx=xGx = xGx=x. (A self-map on SSS is a function GGG from SSS to itself. When working with self-maps it is common to abbreviate G(x)G(x)G(x) to GxGxGx.) In this chapter, we will say that GGG is globally stable on SSS if GGG has a unique fixed point x∗∈Sx^* \in Sx∗∈S and Gkx→x∗G^k x \to x^*Gkx→x∗ as k→∞k \to \inftyk→∞ for all x∈Sx \in Sx∈S. In other words, under this property, the fixed point is not only unique but also globally attracting under iteration of GGG.

We have already discussed fixed points, indirectly or directly, in multiple contexts:

  • In Chapter 2 we studied the equation x=Ax+dx = A x + dx=Ax+d, where xxx is an output vector, AAA is a matrix of coefficients and ddd is a demand vector. A solution xxx to this equation can also be thought of as a fixed point of the affine map Fx=Ax+dFx = Ax + dFx=Ax+d.

  • In Chapter 4 we learned that a stationary distribution of a finite Markov model with state space SSS and adjacency matrix PPP is a ψ∈D(S)\psi \in \dD(S)ψ∈D(S) with ψ=ψP\psi = \psi Pψ=ψP. In other words, ψ\psiψ is a fixed point of ψ↦ψP\psi \mapsto \psi Pψ↦ψP in D(S)\dD(S)D(S).

  • In Chapter 3 we studied the Bellman equation q(x)=min⁡y∈O(x){c(x,y)+q(y)}q(x) = \min_{y \in \oO(x)} \{ c(x, y) + q(y) \}q(x)=miny∈O(x)​{c(x,y)+q(y)} and introduced an operator the Bellman operator TTT, with the property that its fixed points exactly coincide with solutions to the Bellman equation.

In each case, when we introduced these fixed point problems, we immediately needed to consider questions of existence and uniqueness of fixed points. Now we address these same issues more systematically in an abstract setting.

5.1.1Contraction Mappings¶

In Chapter 2 we studied solutions of the system x=Ax+bx = Ax + bx=Ax+b that are fixed points of the affine map Fx=Ax+bFx = Ax + bFx=Ax+b on Rn\RR^nRn studied in Example 5.1.1. The Neumann series lemma is, in essence, a statement about existence and uniqueness of fixed points of this map. Here we investigate another fixed point theorem, due to Stefan Banach (1892–1945), that can be thought of as extending the Neumann series lemma to nonlinear systems.

5.1.1.1Contractions¶

Let SSS be a nonempty subset of Rn\RR^nRn. A self-map FFF on SSS is called contracting or a contraction of modulus λ\lambdaλ on SSS if there exists a λ<1\lambda < 1λ<1 and a norm ∥⋅∥\| \cdot \|∥⋅∥ on Rn\RR^nRn such that

∥Fu−Fv∥⩽λ∥u−v∥for allu,v∈S.\| Fu - Fv \| \leq \lambda \| u - v \| \quad \text{for all} \quad u, v \in S.∥Fu−Fv∥⩽λ∥u−v∥for allu,v∈S.
(5.1)
Exercise 5.1.1

Let FFF be a contraction of modulus λ\lambdaλ on SSS. Show that

  1. FFF is continuous on SSS and

  2. FFF has at most one fixed point on SSS.

Example 5.1.1.

Let S=RnS = \RR^nS=Rn, paired with the Euclidean norm ∥⋅∥\| \cdot \|∥⋅∥. Let Fx=Ax+bFx = Ax + bFx=Ax+b, where A∈Mn×nA \in \matset{n}{n}A∈Mn×n and b∈Rnb \in \RR^nb∈Rn. If ∥A∥<1\| A \| < 1∥A∥<1, where ∥⋅∥\| \cdot \|∥⋅∥ is the operator norm on Mn×n\matset{n}{n}Mn×n, then FFF is a contraction of modulus ∥A∥\| A \|∥A∥, since, for any x,y∈Sx, y \in Sx,y∈S,

∥Ax+b−Ay−b∥=∥A(x−y)∥⩽∥A∥∥x−y∥.\| Ax + b - Ay - b \| = \| A(x - y) \| \leq \|A \| \| x - y \|.∥Ax+b−Ay−b∥=∥A(x−y)∥⩽∥A∥∥x−y∥.

The next example uses a similar idea but is based on a different norm.

Example 5.1.2.

In (2.22) we studied the system ρ=A⊤ρ−ε\rho = A^\top \rho - \epsilonρ=A⊤ρ−ε, where A=(aij)A = (a_{ij})A=(aij​) is a matrix of coefficients satisfying ∑iaij=1−α\sum_i a_{ij} = 1 - \alpha∑i​aij​=1−α for some α∈(0,1)\alpha \in (0,1)α∈(0,1), the vector ε\epsilonε is given and ρ\rhoρ is unknown. Solutions can be viewed as a fixed points of the map F ⁣:Rn→RnF \colon \RR^n \to \RR^nF:Rn→Rn defined by Fp=A⊤p−εF p = A^\top p - \epsilonFp=A⊤p−ε. Under the ∥⋅∥∞\| \cdot \|_\infty∥⋅∥∞​ norm, FFF is a contraction of modulus 1−α1-\alpha1−α on Rn\RR^nRn. Indeed, for any p,q∈Rnp, q \in \RR^np,q∈Rn,

∥Fp−Fq∥∞=max⁡j∣∑i=1naij(pi−qi)∣⩽max⁡j∑i=1naij∣pi−qi∣.\| Fp - Fq \|_\infty = \max_j \left| \sum_{i=1}^n a_{ij} (p_i - q_i) \right| \leq \max_j \sum_{i=1}^n a_{ij} \left| p_i - q_i \right|.∥Fp−Fq∥∞​=jmax​​i=1∑n​aij​(pi​−qi​)​⩽jmax​i=1∑n​aij​∣pi​−qi​∣.

Since ∣pi−qi∣⩽∥p−q∥∞|p_i - q_i| \leq \| p - q \|_\infty∣pi​−qi​∣⩽∥p−q∥∞​, we obtain

∥Fp−Fq∥∞⩽max⁡j∑i=1naij∥p−q∥∞=(1−α)∥p−q∥∞.\| Fp - Fq \|_\infty \leq \max_j \sum_{i=1}^n a_{ij} \| p - q \|_\infty = (1- \alpha) \| p - q \|_\infty.∥Fp−Fq∥∞​⩽jmax​i=1∑n​aij​∥p−q∥∞​=(1−α)∥p−q∥∞​.

Consider again Example 5.1.1. For the affine map Fx=Ax+bFx = Ax + bFx=Ax+b, the condition ∥A∥<1\| A \| < 1∥A∥<1 used to obtain contraction is stronger than the condition r(A)<1r(A) < 1r(A)<1 used to obtain a unique fixed point in the Neumann series lemma (see Exercise 2.3.11). Furthermore, the Neumann series lemma provides a geometric series representation of the fixed point. On the other hand, as we now show, the contraction property can be used to obtain unique fixed points when the map in question is not affine.

5.1.1.2Banach’s Theorem¶

The fundamental importance of contractions stems from the following theorem.

Theorem 5.1.1 (Banach’s contraction mapping theorem).

If SSS is closed in Rn\RR^nRn and FFF is a contraction of modulus λ\lambdaλ on SSS, then FFF has a unique fixed point u∗u^*u∗ in SSS and

∥Fnu−u∗∥⩽λn∥u−u∗∥for all n∈N and u∈S.\| F^n u - u^* \| \leq \lambda^n \| u - u^* \| \quad \text{for all } n \in \NN \text{ and } u \in S.∥Fnu−u∗∥⩽λn∥u−u∗∥for all n∈N and u∈S.
(5.2)

In particular, FFF is globally stable on SSS.

We complete a proof of Theorem 5.1.1 in stages.

∥um−uk∥⩽∑i=mk−1λi∥u0−u1∥\| u_m - u_k \| \leq \sum_{i=m}^{k-1} \lambda^i \| u_0 - u_1 \|∥um​−uk​∥⩽i=m∑k−1​λi∥u0​−u1​∥

holds for all m,k∈Nm, k \in \NNm,k∈N with m<km < km<k.

Hence (um)(u_m)(um​) is Cauchy, as claimed.

Proof of Theorem 5.1.1.

In the exercises we proved existence of a point u∗∈Su^* \in Su∗∈S such that Fmu→u∗F^m u \to u^*Fmu→u∗. The fact that u∗u^*u∗ is a fixed point of FFF now follows from Lemma 6.1.6 and Exercise 5.1.1. Uniqueness is implied by Exercise 5.1.1. The bound (5.2) follows from iteration on the contraction inequality (5.1) while setting v=u∗v=u^*v=u∗. ◻

5.1.1.3Eventual Contractions¶

Let SSS be a nonempty subset of Rn\RR^nRn. A self-map FFF on SSS is called eventually contracting if there exists a k∈Nk \in \NNk∈N such that FkF^kFk is a contraction on SSS. Significantly, most of the conclusions of Banach’s theorem carry over to the case where FFF is eventually contracting.

Theorem 5.1.2.

Let FFF be a self-map on S⊂RnS \subset \RR^nS⊂Rn. If SSS is closed and FFF is eventually contracting, then FFF is globally stable on SSS.

Exercise 5.1.5

Prove Theorem 5.1.2.1

Solution to Exercise 5.1.5

Let SSS be complete, let FFF be a self-map on SSS and let FkF^kFk be a uniform contraction. Let u∗u^*u∗ be the unique fixed point of FkF^kFk. Fix ε>0\epsilon > 0ε>0. We can choose nnn such that ∥FnkFu∗−u∗∥<ε\|F^{nk} F u^* - u^* \| < \epsilon∥FnkFu∗−u∗∥<ε. But then

∥Fu∗−u∗∥=∥FFnku∗−u∗∥=∥FnkFu∗−u∗∥<ε.\| F u^*- u^* \| = \| F F^{nk} u^*- u^*\| = \|F^{nk} F u^* - u^* \| < \epsilon.∥Fu∗−u∗∥=∥FFnku∗−u∗∥=∥FnkFu∗−u∗∥<ε.

Since ε\epsilonε was arbitrary we have ∥Fu∗−u∗∥=0\| F u^*- u^*\| = 0∥Fu∗−u∗∥=0, implying that u∗u^*u∗ is a fixed point of FFF.

Regarding convergence, fix u∈Su \in Su∈S. Given n∈Nn \in \NNn∈N, there exist integers j(n)j(n)j(n) and i(n)i(n)i(n) such that n=j(n)k+i(n)n = j(n) k + i(n)n=j(n)k+i(n), and j(n)→∞j(n) \to \inftyj(n)→∞ as n→∞n \to \inftyn→∞. Hence

∥Fnu−u∗∥=∥Fj(n)k+i(n)u−u∗∥=∥Fj(n)kFi(n)u−u∗∥→0(n→∞),\| F^n u - u^* \| = \| F^{j(n)k + i(n)} u - u^* \| = \| F^{j(n)k} F^{i(n)} u - u^* \| \to 0 \qquad (n \to \infty),∥Fnu−u∗∥=∥Fj(n)k+i(n)u−u∗∥=∥Fj(n)kFi(n)u−u∗∥→0(n→∞),

by the assumptions on FkF^kFk. Convergence implies uniqueness of the fixed point (why?).

There is a close connection between Theorem 5.1.2 and the Neumann series lemma (NSL). If S=RnS=\RR^nS=Rn and Fx=Ax+bF x = A x + bFx=Ax+b with r(A)<1r(A) < 1r(A)<1, then the NSL implies a unique fixed point. We can also obtain this result from Theorem 5.1.2, since, for any k∈Nk \in \NNk∈N,

∥Fkx−Fky∥=∥Akx−Aky∥=∥Ak(x−y)∥⩽∥Ak∥∥x−y∥.\| F^k x - F^k y \| = \| A^k x - A^k y \| = \| A^k (x - y) \| \leq \|A^k \| \| x - y \|.∥Fkx−Fky∥=∥Akx−Aky∥=∥Ak(x−y)∥⩽∥Ak∥∥x−y∥.

As r(A)<1r(A) < 1r(A)<1, we can choose kkk such that ∥Ak∥<1\| A^k \| < 1∥Ak∥<1 (see Section 2.3.3). Hence FFF is eventually contracting and Theorem 5.1.2 applies.

As mentioned above, contractions and eventual contractions have much wider scope than the NSL, since they can also be applied in nonlinear settings. At the same time, the NSL is preferred when its conditions hold, since it also gives inverse and power series representations of the fixed point.

5.1.1.4A Condition for Eventual Contractions¶

The result below provides a useful test for the eventual contraction property. (In the statement, the absolute value of a vector is defined pointwise, as in Section 6.1.2.2.)

Proposition 5.1.3.

Let FFF be a self-map on S⊂RnS \subset \RR^nS⊂Rn such that, for some n×nn \times nn×n matrix AAA,

∣Fx−Fy∣⩽A∣x−y∣for all  x,y∈S.|F x - F y| \leq A | x - y | \quad \text{for all } \, x, y \in S.∣Fx−Fy∣⩽A∣x−y∣for all x,y∈S.

If, in addition, A⩾0A \geq 0A⩾0 and r(A)<1r(A) < 1r(A)<1, then FFF is eventually contracting on SSS with respect to the Euclidean norm.

Proof.

Our first claim is that, under the conditions of the proposition,

∣Fkx−Fky∣⩽Ak∣x−y∣for all k∈N and x,y∈S.|F^k x - F^k y| \leq A^k | x - y | \quad \text{for all } k \in \NN \text{ and } x, y \in S.∣Fkx−Fky∣⩽Ak∣x−y∣for all k∈N and x,y∈S.
(5.3)

This is true at k=1k=1k=1 by assumption. If it is true at k−1k-1k−1, then

∣Fkx−Fky∣⩽A∣Fk−1x−Fk−1y∣⩽AAk−1∣x−y∣,|F^k x - F^k y| \leq A | F^{k-1} x - F^{k-1} y | \leq A A^{k-1} | x - y |,∣Fkx−Fky∣⩽A∣Fk−1x−Fk−1y∣⩽AAk−1∣x−y∣,
(5.4)

where the second inequality uses the induction hypothesis and A⩾0A \geq 0A⩾0 (so that u⩽vu \leq vu⩽v implies Au⩽AvAu \leq AvAu⩽Av). Hence (5.3) holds.

It follows from the definition of the Euclidean norm that ∥∣u∣∥=∥u∥\| |u| \| = \| u\|∥∣u∣∥=∥u∥ for any vector uuu. Also, for the same norm, ∣u∣⩽∣v∣|u| \leq |v|∣u∣⩽∣v∣ implies ∥u∥⩽∥v∥\| u \| \leq \| v\|∥u∥⩽∥v∥. Hence, for all k∈Nk \in \NNk∈N and x,y∈Sx, y \in Sx,y∈S,

∥Fkx−Fky∥⩽∥Ak∣x−y∣∥⩽∥Ak∥o∥x−y∥.\| F^k x - F^k y \| \leq \| A^k |x - y| \| \leq \| A^k \|_o \| x - y \|.∥Fkx−Fky∥⩽∥Ak∣x−y∣∥⩽∥Ak∥o​∥x−y∥.

In the second inequality, we used ∥⋅∥o\| \cdot \|_o∥⋅∥o​ for the operator norm, combined with the fact that ∥Au∥⩽∥A∥o∥u∥\| A u \| \leq \|A\|_o \|u\|∥Au∥⩽∥A∥o​∥u∥ always holds, as discussed in Section 2.3.2.3.

By Gelfand’s lemma (see in particular Exercise 2.3.18), we obtain existence of a λ∈(0,1)\lambda \in (0,1)λ∈(0,1) and a k∈Nk \in \NNk∈N with ∥Ak∥o⩽λ<1\|A^k\|_o \leq \lambda < 1∥Ak∥o​⩽λ<1. Hence, for this kkk,

∥Fkx−Fky∥⩽λ∥x−y∥.\| F^k x - F^k y \| \leq \lambda \|x - y\|.∥Fkx−Fky∥⩽λ∥x−y∥.

Since λ\lambdaλ does not depend on xxx or yyy, we have shown that FFF is an eventual contraction on SSS with respect to the Euclidean norm. ◻

5.1.2Shortest Paths Revisited¶

Consider again the shortest path problem introduced in Section 3.1. One modification that sometimes appears in applications is the addition of discounting during travel between vertices. For example, if the vertices are international ports and travel takes place by sea, then port-to-port travel time is measured in weeks or even months. It is natural to apply time discounting to future costs associated with that travel, to implement the idea that paying a given dollar amount in the future is preferable to paying it now.

Exercise 5.1.6

Suppose it is possible to borrow and lend risk-free at a positive interest rate rrr. Explain why it is always preferable to have $100 now than $100 in a year’s time in this setting.

Solution to Exercise 5.1.6

If the risk-free real interest rate rrr is positive, then $100 received now can be converted with probability one into (1+r)100>100(1+r) 100 > 100(1+r)100>100 dollars in one year.

Recall that, without discounting, the Bellman equation for the shortest path problem takes the form q(x)=min⁡y∈O(x){c(x,y)+q(y)}q(x) = \min_{y \in \oO(x)} \{ c(x, y) + q(y) \}q(x)=miny∈O(x)​{c(x,y)+q(y)} for all x∈Vx \in Vx∈V, where ccc is the cost function VVV is the set of vertices and qqq is a candidate for the cost-to-go function. We showed that the minimum cost-to-go function q∗q^*q∗ satisfies the Bellman equation and is the unique fixed point of the Bellman operator.

The Bellman equation neatly divides the problem into current costs, embedded in the term c(x,y)c(x, y)c(x,y), and future costs embedded in q(y)q(y)q(y). To add discounting, we need only discount q(y)q(y)q(y). We do this by multiplying it by a discount factor β∈(0,1)\beta \in (0, 1)β∈(0,1). The Bellman equation is then q(x)=min⁡y∈O(x){c(x,y)+βq(y)}q(x) = \min_{y \in \oO(x)} \{ c(x, y) + \beta q(y) \}q(x)=miny∈O(x)​{c(x,y)+βq(y)} for all x∈Vx \in Vx∈V and the Bellman operator is

Tq(x)=min⁡y∈O(x){c(x,y)+βq(y)}(x∈V).Tq(x) = \min_{y \in \oO(x)} \{ c(x, y) + \beta q(y) \} \qquad (x \in V).Tq(x)=y∈O(x)min​{c(x,y)+βq(y)}(x∈V).
(5.5)

In Section 3.1.2, without discounting, we had to work hard to show that the Bellman operator has a unique fixed point in UUU, the set of all q ⁣:V→R+q \colon V \to \RR_+q:V→R+​ with q(d)=0q(d)=0q(d)=0. With discounting the proof is easier, since we can leverage the Banach contraction mapping theorem.

In what follows, we identify the vertices in VVV with integers 1,…,n1, \ldots, n1,…,n, where ddd is identified with nnn. We then understand UUU as all nonnegative vectors qqq in Rn\RR^nRn with q(n)=0q(n) = 0q(n)=0. (We continue to write q(x)q(x)q(x) for the xxx-th element of the vector qqq, but now xxx is in [n]\natset{n}[n].)

Prove that UUU is a closed subset of Rn\RR^nRn.

Take qk→qq_k \to qqk​→q where (qk)(q_k)(qk​) is a sequence of nnn-vectors contained in UUU. By Exercise 6.1.8, since qk⩾0q_k \geq 0qk​⩾0 for all kkk, we must have q⩾0q \geq 0q⩾0. It remains only to show that q(n)=0q(n)=0q(n)=0. As qk∈Uq_k \in Uqk​∈U for all kkk, we have qk(n)=0q_k(n)=0qk​(n)=0 for all kkk. By Lemma 2.3.1, we also have qk(n)→q(n)q_k(n) \to q(n)qk​(n)→q(n). Hence q(n)=0q(n)=0q(n)=0.

Exercise 5.1.8

Prove that TTT is order-preserving on UUU with respect to the pointwise order.

Solution to Exercise 5.1.8

We need to show that if p,q∈Up, q \in Up,q∈U and p⩽qp \leq qp⩽q, then Tp⩽TqTp \leq TqTp⩽Tq. This follows easily from the definition of TTT in (5.5).

Exercise 5.1.9

Prove that, for any q∈Uq \in Uq∈U and α∈R+\alpha \in \RR_+α∈R+​, we have T(q+α1)=Tq+βα1T(q + \alpha \1) = Tq + \beta \alpha \1T(q+α1)=Tq+βα1.

Solution to Exercise 5.1.9

Fix q∈Uq \in Uq∈U, α∈R+\alpha \in \RR_+α∈R+​ and x∈Vx \in Vx∈V. By definition,

T(q+α1)(x)=min⁡y∈O(x){c(x,y)+βq(y)+αβ}=Tq(x)+αβ.T(q + \alpha \1) (x) = \min_{y \in \oO(x)} \{ c(x, y) + \beta q(y) + \alpha \beta \} = Tq(x) + \alpha \beta.T(q+α1)(x)=y∈O(x)min​{c(x,y)+βq(y)+αβ}=Tq(x)+αβ.

Hence T(q+α1)=Tq+βα1T(q + \alpha \1) = Tq + \beta \alpha \1T(q+α1)=Tq+βα1 as claimed.

Now let ∥⋅∥∞\| \cdot \|_\infty∥⋅∥∞​ be the supremum norm on Rn\RR^nRn (see Section 2.3.1). We claim that TTT is a contraction on UUU of modulus β\betaβ. To see that this is so, fix p,q∈Up, q \in Up,q∈U and observe that, pointwise,

Tq=T(p+q−p)⩽T(p+∥q−p∥∞1)⩽Tp+β∥q−p∥∞1,Tq = T(p + q - p) \leq T(p + \|q - p\|_\infty \1) \leq Tp + \beta \|q - p\|_\infty \1,Tq=T(p+q−p)⩽T(p+∥q−p∥∞​1)⩽Tp+β∥q−p∥∞​1,

where the first inequality is by the order-preserving of TTT and the second follows from Exercise 5.1.9. Hence

Tq−Tp⩽β∥q−p∥∞1.Tq - Tp \leq \beta \|q - p\|_\infty \1.Tq−Tp⩽β∥q−p∥∞​1.

∣Tq(x)−Tp(x)∣⩽β∥q−p∥∞|Tq (x) - Tp(x) | \leq \beta \|q - p\|_\infty∣Tq(x)−Tp(x)∣⩽β∥q−p∥∞​

for all x∈[n]x \in \natset{n}x∈[n]. Taking the maximum on the left hand side yields ∥Tq−Tp∥∞⩽β∥q−p∥∞\|Tq - Tp \|_\infty \leq \beta \|q - p\|_\infty∥Tq−Tp∥∞​⩽β∥q−p∥∞​, which shows that TTT is a contraction of modulus β\betaβ. Hence Banach’s theorem applies and a unique fixed point exists.

5.1.3Supply Constraints¶

While the input-output model from Section 2.1.2 has many useful applications, its linear structure can be a liability. One natural objection to linearity is supply constraints: if sector jjj doubles its orders from sector iii, we cannot always expect that sector iii will quickly meet this jump in demand.

In this sector we investigate the impact of supply constraints on equilibrium. These constraints introduce nonlinear relationships between nodes that affect equilibria and make analysis more challenging.

We recall from Section 2.1.2 that did_idi​ is final demand for good iii, xix_ixi​ is total sales of sector iii, zijz_{ij}zij​ is inter-industry sales from sector iii to sector jjj, and aij=zij/xja_{ij} = z_{ij}/x_jaij​=zij​/xj​ is dollar value of inputs from iii per dollar output from jjj.

Departing from our previous formulation of equilibrium in the input-output model, suppose that, in the short run, the total output value of sector iii is constrained by positive constant xˉ(i)\bar x(i)xˉ(i). Holding prices fixed (in the short run), this means that sector iii has a capacity constraint in terms of unit output. For the purposes of our model, the vector of capacity constraints xˉ:=(xˉ(i))i=1n\bar x := (\bar x(i))_{i=1}^nxˉ:=(xˉ(i))i=1n​ can be any vector in R+n\RR^n_+R+n​.

For each sector iii, we modify the accounting identity (2.1) to

xi=min⁡{∑j=1noij+di,  xˉ(i)},x_i = \min \left\{ \sum_{j=1}^n o_{ij} + d_i, \; \bar x(i) \right\},xi​=min{j=1∑n​oij​+di​,xˉ(i)},

where oijo_{ij}oij​ is the value of orders from sector iii made by sector jjj. Thus, if the capacity constraint in sector iii is not binding, then output is the sum of orders from other sectors and orders from final consumers. If xˉ(i)\bar x(i)xˉ(i) is less than this sum, however, then sector iii produces to capacity xˉ(i)\bar x(i)xˉ(i).

An equilibrium for this model is one where all orders are met, subject to capacity constraints. The fact that orders are met means that oij=zij=aijxjo_{ij} = z_{ij} = a_{ij} x_joij​=zij​=aij​xj​. Substituting this equality into (5.6) and rewriting as a vector equality, (5.6) can equivalently be formulated as

x=GxwhereGx:=(Ax+d)∧xˉ.x = G x \quad \text{where} \quad G x := (A x + d) \wedge \bar x.x=GxwhereGx:=(Ax+d)∧xˉ.

5.1.4Fixed Points and Monotonicity¶

Banach’s fixed point theorem and its extensions are foundations of many central results in pure and applied mathematics. For our purposes, however, we need to search a little further, since not all mappings generated by network models have the contraction property. In this section, we investigate two fixed point results that drop contractivity in favor of monotonicity.

5.1.4.1Existence¶

Without contractivity, one needs to work harder to obtain even existence of fixed points, let alone uniqueness and convergence. This is especially true if the map in question fails to be continuous. If, however, the map is order preserving, then existence can often be obtained via some variation on the Knaster–Tarski fixed point theorem.

Here we present a version of this existence result that is optimized to our setting, while avoiding unnecessary excursions into order theory. In stating the theorem, we recall that a closed order interval in Rn\RR^nRn is a set of the form

[a,b]:={x∈Rn:a⩽x⩽b}[a, b] := \setntn{x \in \RR^n}{a \leq x \leq b}[a,b]:={x∈Rn:a⩽x⩽b}

where aaa and bbb are vectors in Rn\RR^nRn. Also, we call (xk)⊂Rn(x_k) \subset \RR^n(xk​)⊂Rn increasing (resp., decreasing) if xk⩽xk+1x_k \leq x_{k+1}xk​⩽xk+1​ (resp., xk⩾xk+1x_k \geq x_{k+1}xk​⩾xk+1​) for all kkk.

5.1.4.2Du’s Theorem¶

Theorem 5.1.5 is useful because of its relatively weak assumptions. At the same time, it fails to deliver uniqueness. Hence its conclusions are considerably weaker than the results we obtained from contractivity assumptions in Section 5.1.1.

In order to recover uniqueness without imposing contractivity, we now consider order-preserving maps that have additional shape properties. In doing so, we use the definition of concave and convex functions in Section 6.1.5.2.

Theorem 5.1.6 (Du).

Let GGG be an order-preserving self-map on order interval S=[a,b]⊂RnS = [a, b] \subset \RR^nS=[a,b]⊂Rn. In this setting, if either

  1. GGG is concave and Ga≫aG a \gg aGa≫a or

  2. GGG is convex and Gb≪bG b \ll bGb≪b,

then GGG is globally stable on SSS.

A proof of Theorem 5.1.6 was obtained in an more abstract setting in Du (1990). Interested readers can consult that article for a proof.

To illustrate how these results can be applied, consider the constrained production model without assuming positive value added, so that r(A)<1r(A) < 1r(A)<1 is not enforced. In Exercise 5.1.12 we obtained existence. With Theorem 5.1.6 in hand, we can also show uniqueness whenever d≫0d \gg 0d≫0 and xˉ≫0\bar x \gg 0xˉ≫0.

Indeed, we have already seen that GGG is a self-map on S:=[0,xˉ]S := [0, \bar x]S:=[0,xˉ] and, when this last condition holds, we have G0=d∧xˉ≫0G 0 = d \wedge \bar x \gg 0G0=d∧xˉ≫0. Hence the conclusions of Theorem 5.1.6 will hold if we can establish that GGG is concave.

5.2Financial Networks¶

Given the long history of crises in financial markets around the globe, economists and business analysts have developed many tools for assessing the credit-worthiness of banks and other financial institutions. After the major financial crises of 2007-2008, originating in the subprime market in the US and the sudden collapse of Lehmann Brothers, it became clear that the financial health of individual institutions cannot be assessed in isolation. Rather, it is essential to analyze solvency and credit-worthiness in terms of the entire network of claims and liabilities within a highly interconnected financial system. In this section, we review financial crises and apply network analysis to study how they evolve.

5.2.1Contagion¶

Some financial crises have obvious causes external to the banking sector. A prominent example is the hyperinflation that occurred in Weimar Germany around 1921–1923, which was driven by mass printing of bank notes to meet war reparations imposed under the Treaty of Versailles. Here the monetary authority played the central role, while the actions of private banks were more passive.

Other crises seem to form within the financial sector itself, driven by interactions between banks, hedge funds, and asset markets. In many cases, the crisis follows a boom, where asset prices rise and economic growth is strong. Typically, the seeds of the crisis are laid during this boom phase, when banks extend loans and firms raise capital on the basis of progressively more speculative business plans. At some point it becomes clear to investors that these businesses will fail to meet expectations, leading to a rush for the exit.

The last phase of this cycle is painful for the financial sector, since rapidly falling asset values force banks and other financial institutions to generate short-term capital by liquidating long-term loans, typically with large losses, as well as selling assets in the face of falling prices, hoarding cash and refusing to roll over or extend short term loans to other institutions in the financial sector. The financial crisis of 2007–2008 provides a textbook example of these dynamics.

One key aspect of the financial crisis of 2007–2008, as well as other similar crises, is contagion, which refers to the way that financial stress spreads across a network of financial institutions. If one institution becomes stressed, that stress will often spread to investors or counterparties to which this institution is indebted. The result of this process is not easy to predict, since, like equilibrium in the production networks studied in Chapter 2, there is a tail chasing problem: stress spreads from institution AAA to institutions BBB, CCC and DDD, which may in turn increase stress on AAA, and so on.

In this section we study financial contagion, beginning with a now-standard model of default cascades.

5.2.2Default Cascades¶

Default cascades are a form of financial contagion, in which default by a node in a network leads to default by some of its counterparties, which then spreads across the network. Below we present a model of default cascades and analyze its equilibria.

5.2.2.1Network Valuation¶

Consider a financial network G=(V,E,w)\gG = (V, E, w)G=(V,E,w), where V=[n]V = \natset{n}V=[n] is a list of nnn financial institutions called banks, with an edge (i,j)∈E(i, j) \in E(i,j)∈E indicating that jjj has extended credit to iii. The size of that loan is w(i,j)w(i, j)w(i,j). Thus, an edge points in the direction of a liability, as in Figure 1.17: edge (i,j)(i, j)(i,j) indicates a liability for iii and an asset for jjj. As in Section 1.4.1, the set of all direct predecessors of i∈Vi \in Vi∈V will be written as I(i)\iI(i)I(i), while the set of all direct successors will be denoted O(i)\oO(i)O(i).

Banks in the network have both internal and external liabilities, as well as internal and external assets. Internal (i.e., interbank) liabilities and assets are given by the weight function www, in the sense that w(i,j)w(i,j)w(i,j) is a liability for iii, equal to the size of its loan from jjj, and also an asset for jjj. Positive weights indicate the presence of counterparty risk: when jjj holds an asset of book value w(i,j)w(i, j)w(i,j), whether or not the loan is repaid in full depends on the stress placed on bank iii and rules that govern repayment in the event of insolvency.

We use the following notation for the primitives of the model: xi:=∑j∈O(i)w(i,j)x_i := \sum_{j \in \oO(i)} w(i, j)xi​:=∑j∈O(i)​w(i,j) is total interbank liabilities of bank iii,

Πij:={w(i,j)/xi if xi>00 otherwise\Pi_{ij} := \begin{cases} w(i, j) / x_i & \text{ if } x_i > 0 \\ 0 & \text{ otherwise} \end{cases}Πij​:={w(i,j)/xi​0​ if xi​>0 otherwise​
(5.9)

is the matrix of relative interbank liabilities, aia_iai​ is external assets held by bank iii and did_idi​ is external liabilities.

When considering the interbank assets of bank jjj, we need to distinguish between the book value ∑i∈I(j)w(i,j)\sum_{i \in \iI(j)} w(i, j)∑i∈I(j)​w(i,j) of its claims on other banks and the realized value in the face of partial or complete default by its counterparties I(j)\iI(j)I(j). To this end, we introduce a clearing vector p∈R+np \in \RR^n_+p∈R+n​, which is a list of proposed payments by each bank in the network. In particular, pip_ipi​ is total payments made by bank iii to its counterparties within the banking sector. Under the choice of a particular clearing vector, the actual payments received by bank jjj on its internal loan portfolio are ∑i∈VpiΠij\sum_{i \in V} p_i \Pi_{ij}∑i∈V​pi​Πij​.

The last statement is an assumption about the legal framework for the banking sector. It means that the actual payment piΠijp_i \Pi_{ij}pi​Πij​ from iii to jjj is proportional to the amount that iii owes jjj, relative to its total interbank obligations. The idea is that all counterparties in the banking sector have equal seniority, so that residual funds are spread across claimants according to the relative size of the claims.

Let p^j\hat p_jp^​j​ be the amount of funds bank jjj makes available to repay all of its debts, both interbank and external. This quantity is

p^j=min⁡{aj+∑i∈VpiΠij,  dj+xj}.\hat p_j = \min \left\{ a_j + \sum_{i \in V} p_i \Pi_{ij}, \; d_j + x_j \right\}.p^​j​=min{aj​+i∈V∑​pi​Πij​,dj​+xj​}.
(5.10)

The right hand term inside the min⁡\minmin operator is total debts of bank jjj. The left hand side is the amount on hand to repay those debts, including external assets and repayments by other banks. The bank repays up to—but not beyond—its ability to pay.

External liabilities are assumed to be senior to interbank liabilities, which means that for bank jjj we also have

pj=max⁡{p^j−dj,  0}.p_j = \max\{\hat p_j - d_j, \; 0\}.pj​=max{p^​j​−dj​,0}.
(5.11)

Thus, interbank payments by jjj are a remainder after external debts are settled. If these debts exceed the bank’s ability to pay, the bank becomes insolvent and pays nothing to internal creditors. This is a form of limited liability.

Combining (5.10) and (5.11) and rearranging slightly yields

pj=max⁡{min⁡{aj−dj+∑i∈VpiΠij,  xj},  0}p_j = \max \left\{ \min \left\{ a_j - d_j + \sum_{i \in V} p_i \Pi_{ij}, \; x_j \right\}, \; 0 \right\}pj​=max{min{aj​−dj​+i∈V∑​pi​Πij​,xj​},0}

Now let’s take ppp, aaa, ddd and xxx as row vectors in Rn\RR^nRn and write this collection of equations, indexed of jjj, in vector form. With max⁡\maxmax and min⁡\minmin taken pointwise, and using the symbols ∨\vee∨ and ∧\wedge∧ for max and min, we get

p=((a−d+pΠ)∧x)∨0.p = ((a - d + p\Pi) \wedge x) \vee 0.p=((a−d+pΠ)∧x)∨0.
(5.12)

A solution to this equation is called an equilibrium clearing vector for the banking system.

Remark 5.2.1.

An equilibrium clearing vector captures impacts of contagion within the specified banking system, in the sense that it traces out the full network effects of interbank lending within the model. We shall study this equilibrium, while also recognizing that the model is restrictive in the sense that it assumes a specific form for seniority and implicitly rules out some kinds of nonlinear phenomena. We return to this theme in Section 5.2.3.

5.2.2.2Existence and Uniqueness of Fixed Points¶

In order to analyze existence and uniqueness of equilibria, we introduce the operator T ⁣:Rn→RnT \colon \RR^n \to \RR^nT:Rn→Rn defined by

Tp=((e+pΠ)∧x)∨0,Tp = ((e + p\Pi) \wedge x) \vee 0,Tp=((e+pΠ)∧x)∨0,
(5.13)

where e:=a−de := a - de:=a−d represents net external assets. Evidently p∈R+np \in \RR^n_+p∈R+n​ is an equilibrium clearing vector if and only if it is a fixed point of TTT.

Exercise 5.2.1

Prove that the operator TTT is continuous on Rn\RR^nRn.

Solution to Exercise 5.2.1

In essence, this holds because compositions of continuous functions are continuous. Nonetheless, here is a more explicit proof: Recalling the inequalities in Section 6.1.1.1, applied pointwise to vectors, we have, for any p,q∈Rnp, q \in \RR^np,q∈Rn,

∣Tp−Tq∣⩽∣(e+pΠ)∧x)−(e+qΠ)∧x)∣⩽∣(p−q)Π∣.|Tp - Tq| \leq | (e + p\Pi) \wedge x) - (e + q\Pi) \wedge x) | \leq | (p - q) \Pi |.∣Tp−Tq∣⩽∣(e+pΠ)∧x)−(e+qΠ)∧x)∣⩽∣(p−q)Π∣.

Since, for the Euclidean norm, ∥∣u∣∥=∥u∥\| |u| \| = \| u\|∥∣u∣∥=∥u∥ and u,v⩾0u, v \geq 0u,v⩾0 with u⩽vu \leq vu⩽v implies ∥u∥⩽∥v∥\| u \| \leq \| v\|∥u∥⩽∥v∥, we then have ∥Tp−Tq∥⩽∥(p−q)Π∥⩽∥p−q∥∥Π∥o\|Tp - Tq\| \leq \| (p - q) \Pi \| \leq \| p - q \| \| \Pi \|_o∥Tp−Tq∥⩽∥(p−q)Π∥⩽∥p−q∥∥Π∥o​. It follows easily that if ∥pn−p∥→0\| p_n - p \| \to 0∥pn​−p∥→0, then ∥Tpn−Tp∥→0\|Tp_n - Tp\| \to 0∥Tpn​−Tp∥→0 also holds.

Using this operator, establishing existence of at least one equilibrium clearing vector is not problematic for this model, regardless of the values of the primitives and configuration of the network:

Exercise 5.2.2

Show that the banking model described above always has at least one equilibrium clearing vector. What else can you say about equilibria in this general case?

Solution to Exercise 5.2.2

Since Π⩾0\Pi \geq 0Π⩾0, we always have pΠ⩽qΠp \Pi \leq q \PipΠ⩽qΠ whenever p⩽qp \leq qp⩽q. As a result, p↦a−d+pΠp \mapsto a - d + p \Pip↦a−d+pΠ is order-preserving and hence so is TTT. What else can we say about equilibria in this setting? By the same theorem, TTT has a least fixed point p∗p^*p∗ and a greatest fixed point p∗∗p^{**}p∗∗ in SSS. Moreover, since TTT is continuous, Tk0↑p∗T^k 0 \uparrow p^*Tk0↑p∗ and Tkx↓p∗∗T^k x \downarrow p^{**}Tkx↓p∗∗.

While existence is automatic in this model, uniqueness is not:

Example 5.2.1.

If n=2n=2n=2, e=(0,0)e=(0, 0)e=(0,0) and (1,1)(1, 1)(1,1) and Π=(0110)\Pi = \begin{pmatrix} 0 & 1 \\ 1 & 0 \end{pmatrix}Π=(01​10​), then Tp=pTp = pTp=p is equivalent to

There are several approaches to proving uniqueness of fixed points of TTT. Here is one:

Exercise 5.2.3

Prove that TTT is globally stable on S:=[0,x]S := [0, x]S:=[0,x] whenever r(Π)<1r(\Pi) < 1r(Π)<1.2

Solution to Exercise 5.2.3

Fix p,q∈Sp, q \in Sp,q∈S. Using the inequalities for min and max in Section 6.1.1.1, applied pointwise, we have

∣Tp−Tq∣⩽∣e+pΠ−(e+qΠ)∣=∣(p−q)Π∣⩽∣p−q∣Π|Tp - Tq| \leq |e + p \Pi - (e + q\Pi)| = |(p-q) \Pi| \leq |p-q| \Pi∣Tp−Tq∣⩽∣e+pΠ−(e+qΠ)∣=∣(p−q)Π∣⩽∣p−q∣Π

After transposing both sides of this equation, we see that, when r(Π)<1r(\Pi)<1r(Π)<1, the conditions of of Proposition 5.1.3 hold. The result follows. (If you prefer, instead of taking transposes, just use the proof of Proposition 5.1.3 directly, modified slightly to use the fact that we are operating on row vectors.)

This leads us to the following result:

Proposition 5.2.1.

Let G\gGG be a financial network. If, for each bank i∈Vi \in Vi∈V, there exists a bank j∈Vj \in Vj∈V with i→ji \to ji→j and such that jjj has zero interbank liabilities, then TTT is globally stable on SSS and G\gGG has a unique equilibrium clearing vector.

Proof.

By construction, the matrix Π\PiΠ is substochastic. Suppose that Π\PiΠ is also weakly chained substochastic. Then, by Proposition 2.3.5, we have r(Π)<1r(\Pi)<1r(Π)<1 and, by Exercise 5.2.3, TTT is globally stable on SSS. Hence the proof will be complete if we can show that, under the stated conditions, Π\PiΠ is weakly chained substochastic.

To see that this is so, let G\gGG be a financial network that satisfies the conditions of Proposition 5.2.1. Now fix i∈Vi \in Vi∈V. We know that there exists a bank j∈Vj \in Vj∈V with i→ji \to ji→j and jjj has no interbank liabilities. If w(i,j)>0w(i,j) > 0w(i,j)>0, then Πij>0\Pi_{ij} > 0Πij​>0, so i→ji \to ji→j under digraph G\gGG implies i→ji \to ji→j in the digraph induced by the substochastic matrix Π\PiΠ. Also, since jjj has no interbank liabilities, we have xj=0x_j = 0xj​=0, and hence row jjj of Π\PiΠ is identically zero. In particular, ∑kΠjk=0\sum_k \Pi_{jk} = 0∑k​Πjk​=0. Hence Π\PiΠ is weakly chained substochastic, as required. ◻

Remark 5.2.2.

The proof of Proposition 5.2.1 also shows that TTT is eventually contracting, so we can compute the unique fixed point by taking the limit of TkpT^k pTkp for any choice of p∈Sp \in Sp∈S.

There are several possible assumptions about the structure of the bank network G\gGG that imply the conditions of Proposition 5.2.1. For example, it would be enough that G\gGG is strongly connected and has at least one bank with zero interbank liabilities. Below we investigate another sufficient condition, related to cyclicality.

Exercise 5.2.4

Let G\gGG be a financial network. Show that G\gGG has a unique equilibrium clearing vector whenever G\gGG is a directed acyclic graph.

Solution to Exercise 5.2.4

Let G=(V,E,w)\gG = (V, E, w)G=(V,E,w) be a financial network and a directed acyclic graph. By Proposition 5.2.1, it suffices to show that, for each bank i∈Vi \in Vi∈V, there exists a bank j∈Vj \in Vj∈V with i→ji \to ji→j and such that jjj has zero interbank liabilities. To this end, fix i∈Vi \in Vi∈V. By the directed acyclic graph property, we know that there exists a j∈Vj \in Vj∈V with i→ji \to ji→j and O(j)=0\oO(j)=0O(j)=0. But if O(j)=0\oO(j)=0O(j)=0, then jjj has no interbank liabilities. The claim follows.

5.2.2.3Nonnegative External Equity¶

In this section we investigate the special case in which

(E1) each bank has nonzero interbank debt, so that Π\PiΠ is a stochastic matrix, and

(E2) external net assets are nonnegative, in the sense that e=a−d⩾0e = a - d \geq 0e=a−d⩾0.

In view of (E1), we cannot hope to use Proposition 5.2.1, since we always have r(Π)=1r(\Pi)=1r(Π)=1 when Π\PiΠ is stochastic. Nonetheless, we can still obtain global stability under certain restrictions on eee and the topology of the network. Here is a relatively straightforward example, which we will later try to refine:

Exercise 5.2.5

By an argument identical to that employed for Exercise 5.1.13, TTT is a concave operator on S=[0,x]S = [0, x]S=[0,x]. Evidently TTT is order preserving. Finally, by (E1), we have xi>0x_i > 0xi​>0 for all iii, so x≫0x \gg 0x≫0 and hence T0=e∧x≫0T0 = e \wedge x \gg 0T0=e∧x≫0. It now follows directly from Du’s theorem that TTT has a unique fixed point in SSS.

The condition e≫0e \gg 0e≫0 is rather strict. Fortunately, it turns out that we can obtain global stability under significantly weaker conditions. To this end, we will say that node jjj in a financial system G\gGG, is cash accessible if there exists an i∈Vi \in Vi∈V such that i→ji \to ji→j and e(i)>0e(i) > 0e(i)>0. In other words, jjj is downstream in the liability chain from at least one bank with positive net assets outside of the banking sector.

Lemma 5.2.2.

Proof.

Let G\gGG be as described. By Corollary 5.1.7, it suffices to show that TTT is an order-preserving concave self-map on [0,x][0,x][0,x] with Tk0≫0T^k 0 \gg 0Tk0≫0 for some k∈Nk \in \NNk∈N. Stronger results are available, with a small amount of effort. In fact, under (E1)–(E2), there is a strong sense in which uniqueness of the fixed point is obtained without any further assumptions, provided that we rule out an ambiguity related to what happens when e=0e=0e=0. That ambiguity is discussed in the next exercise and further references can be found in Section 5.3.

Exercise 5.2.7

Exercise 5.2.8

Let PPP be the set of all nodes in VVV that are cash accessible. Let AAA be all iii in PcP^cPc such that PPP is accessible from iii. Let NNN be all iii in PcP^cPc such that PPP is not accessible from iii. Note that V=P∪A∪NV = P \cup A \cup NV=P∪A∪N and that these sets are disjoint. Show that NNN and PPP are both absorbing sets.

Solution to Exercise 5.2.8

The set NNN is an absorbing set, since, by definition, PPP is not accessible from NNN, and AAA cannot be accessible because otherwise PPP would also be accessible. The set PPP is also absorbing because, if j∈Pcj \in P^cj∈Pc is accessible from some i∈Pi \in Pi∈P, then jjj is cash accessible. But then j∈Pj \in Pj∈P, which is a contradiction.

5.2.3Equity-Cross Holdings¶

In this section we analyze the model of default cascades constructed by Elliott et al., 2014. The model differs from the one studied in Section 5.2.2 in several ways. One is that financial institutions are linked by share cross-holdings: firm iii owns a fraction cijc_{ij}cij​ of firm jjj for i,j∈V:=[n]i, j \in V := \natset{n}i,j∈V:=[n]. This implies that failure of firm jjj reduces the market value of firm iii, which in turn reduces the market value of other firms, and so on.

The second—and ultimately more significant—difference is the introduction of failure costs that add significant nonlinearities to the model. Failure costs reinforce the impact of each firm failure, leading to greater shock propagation across the network. This feature ties into the intuitive idea that, when many firms are financially stressed, a failure by one firm can trigger a wave of bankruptcies.

5.2.3.1Book and Market Value¶

We now describe the features of the model. Let C=(cij)i,j∈VC = (c_{ij})_{i, j \in V}C=(cij​)i,j∈V​ be the matrix of fractional cross-holdings, as mentioned above, with 0⩽cij⩽10 \leq c_{ij} \leq 10⩽cij​⩽1 for all i,ji,ji,j.

Assumption 5.2.1.

The matrix of cross-holdings satisfies ∑kcki<1\sum_k c_{ki} < 1∑k​cki​<1 for all i∈Vi \in Vi∈V.

Assumption 5.2.1 implies that firms are not solely owned by other firms in the network: investors outside the network hold at least some fraction of firm iii for all iii.

The book value of firm iii is given by

bi=ei+∑jcijbj(i∈V).b_i = e_i + \sum_j c_{ij} b_j \qquad (i \in V).bi​=ei​+j∑​cij​bj​(i∈V).
(5.15)

Here the first term ei⩾0e_i \geq 0ei​⩾0 is external assets of firm iii and the second represents the value of firm iii’s cross-holdings. In vector form, the last equation becomes b=e+Cbb = e + C bb=e+Cb.

5.2.3.2Failure Costs¶

So far the model is very straightforward, with the market value of firms being linear in external assets eee. However, since bankruptcy proceedings are expensive, it is reasonable to assume that firm failures are costly. Moreover, when the market value of a firm falls significantly, the firm will experience difficulty raising short term funds, and will often need to cease revenue generating activities and sell illiquid assets well below their potential value.

We now introduce failure costs. As before, vˉi\bar v_ivˉi​ is market value without failure costs, as determined in (5.17), while viv_ivi​ will represent market value in the presence of failure costs. Failure costs for firm iii are modeled as a threshold function

f(vi)=β1{vi<θvˉi}(i=1,…,n),f(v_i) = \beta \1\{v_i < \theta \bar v_i\} \qquad (i = 1, \ldots, n),f(vi​)=β1{vi​<θvˉi​}(i=1,…,n),

where θ∈(0,1)\theta \in (0, 1)θ∈(0,1) and β>0\beta > 0β>0 are parameters. Thus, costs are zero when viv_ivi​ is large and −β-\beta−β when they fall below the threshold θvˉi\theta \bar v_iθvˉi​. In particular, a discrete failure cost of −β-\beta−β is incurred when firm value falls far enough below the no-failure market value vˉi\bar v_ivˉi​. The larger is θ\thetaθ, more prone firms are to failure.

The book value of firm iii without failure costs was defined in (5.15). The book value of firm iii in the presence of failure costs is defined as

bi=ei+∑jcijbj−f(vi).b_i = e_i + \sum_j c_{ij} b_j - f(v_i).bi​=ei​+j∑​cij​bj​−f(vi​).

Written in vector form, with fff applied pointwise to the vector vvv, we get b=e+Cb−f(v)b = e + C b - f (v)b=e+Cb−f(v). Solving for bbb gives b=(I−C)−1(e−f(v))b = (I-C)^{-1} (e - f (v))b=(I−C)−1(e−f(v)). The corresponding market value is

v=Rb=A(e−f(v)).v = R b = A (e - f(v)).v=Rb=A(e−f(v)).
(5.18)

Notice that, when no firms fail, we have vi=vˉiv_i = \bar v_ivi​=vˉi​, as expected.

5.2.3.3Equilibria¶

Equation (5.18) is a nonlinear equation in nnn unknowns. A vector v∈Rnv \in \RR^nv∈Rn solves (5.18) if and only if it is a fixed point of the operator T ⁣:Rn→RnT \colon \RR^n \to \RR^nT:Rn→Rn defined by

Tv=A(e−f(v)).Tv = A (e - f(v)).Tv=A(e−f(v)).
(5.19)

In what follows we set d:=A(e−β1)d := A(e - \beta \1)d:=A(e−β1) and S:=[d,vˉ]S := [d, \bar v]S:=[d,vˉ].

Proposition 5.2.3.

TTT is a self-map on SSS with least fixed point v∗v^*v∗ and greatest fixed point v∗∗v^{**}v∗∗ in SSS. Moreover,

  1. the sequence (Tkd)k∈N(T^k d)_{k \in \NN}(Tkd)k∈N​ converges up to v∗v^*v∗ in a finite number of steps and

  2. the sequence (Tkvˉ)k∈N(T^k \bar v)_{k \in \NN}(Tkvˉ)k∈N​ converges down to v∗∗v^{**}v∗∗ in a finite number of steps.

Note that v∗=v∗∗v^* = v^{**}v∗=v∗∗ is a possibility, in which case TTT has a unique fixed point in SSS.

Exercise 5.2.12

Prove the first claim (first sentence) in Proposition 5.2.3.

Solution to Exercise 5.2.12

Observe that vi⩽vi′v_i \leq v'_ivi​⩽vi′​ implies f(vi)⩾f(vi′)f(v_i) \geq f(v'_i)f(vi​)⩾f(vi′​). As a result, the vector-valued map v↦−f(v)v \mapsto - f(v)v↦−f(v) is order-preserving, and hence so is TTT. Moreover, for v∈[d,vˉ]v \in [d, \bar v]v∈[d,vˉ], we have

d=A(e−β1)⩽Tv:=A(e−f(v))⩽Ae=vˉ,d = A(e - \beta \1) \leq Tv := A (e - f(v)) \leq A e = \bar v,d=A(e−β1)⩽Tv:=A(e−f(v))⩽Ae=vˉ,

so TTT is a self-map on [d,vˉ][d , \bar v][d,vˉ]. It follows directly from Theorem 5.1.5 that TTT has a least and greatest fixed point in SSS.

Why does (Tkd)k∈N(T^k d)_{k \in \NN}(Tkd)k∈N​ converge up to v∗v^*v∗ in a finite number of steps? First, as you saw in the solution to Exercise 5.2.12, the map TTT is an order-preserving self-map on [d,vˉ][d, \bar v][d,vˉ], so Td∈[d,vˉ]Td \in [d, \bar v]Td∈[d,vˉ]. In particular, d⩽Tdd \leq Tdd⩽Td. Iterating on this inequality and using the order-preserving property gives d⩽Td⩽T2d⩽⋯d \leq Td \leq T^2 d \leq \cdotsd⩽Td⩽T2d⩽⋯, so (Tkd)(T^k d)(Tkd) is indeed increasing. Moreover, the range of TTT is a finite set, corresponding to all vectors of the form

u=A(e−βw),u = A(e - \beta w),u=A(e−βw),

where www is an nnn-vector containing only zeros and ones. Finiteness holds because there are only finitely many binary sequences of length nnn.

Exercise 5.2.13

Given the above facts, prove that (Tkd)k∈N(T^k d)_{k \in \NN}(Tkd)k∈N​ converges up to v∗v^*v∗ in a finite number of steps.

Solution to Exercise 5.2.13

First, vk:=Tkdv_k := T^k dvk​:=Tkd is increasing, as just discussed. Second, this sequence can take only finitely many values, since TTT has finite range. As (vk)(v_k)(vk​) is increasing, it cannot cycle, so it must converge in finitely many steps. Let v′v'v′ be this limiting value and let KKK be the number of steps required for (vk)(v_k)(vk​) to attain v′v'v′. Since vk=v′v_k = v'vk​=v′ for all k⩾Kk \geq Kk⩾K, we have

Tv′=TTKv′=TK+1v′=v′,T v' = T T^K v' = T^{K+1} v' = v',Tv′=TTKv′=TK+1v′=v′,

so v′v'v′ is a fixed point of TTT in SSS. Moreover, if v′′v''v′′ is any other fixed point of TTT in SSS, then d⩽v′′d \leq v''d⩽v′′ and hence, by the order-preserving property, vk=Tkd⩽Tkv′′=v′′v_k = T^k d \leq T^k v'' = v''vk​=Tkd⩽Tkv′′=v′′ for all kkk. Hence v′⩽v′′v' \leq v''v′⩽v′′. Thus, v′v'v′ is the least fixed point of TTT.

Similar logic can be applied to prove that (Tkvˉ)k∈N(T^k \bar v)_{k \in \NN}(Tkvˉ)k∈N​ converges down to v∗∗v^{**}v∗∗ in a finite number of steps.

If we set v0=vˉv^0 = \bar vv0=vˉ and vk+1=Tvkv^{k+1} = T v^kvk+1=Tvk, we can consider the sequence of valuations (vk)(v^k)(vk) as a dynamic process, and the number of currently failing firms mk:=∑i1{vik<θ}m^k := \sum_i \1\{v^k_i < \theta\}mk:=∑i​1{vik​<θ} can be understood as tracking waves of bankruptcies. Failures of firms in the first wave put stress on otherwise healthy firms that have exposure to the failed firms, which in turn causes further failures and so on.

Exercise 5.2.14

Prove that the sequence (mk)(m_k)(mk​) is monotone increasing.

As discussed in Proposition 5.2.3, the sequence (vk)(v^k)(vk), which can also be written as (Tkvˉ)(T^k \bar v)(Tkvˉ), is decreasing pointwise. In other words, the value of each firm is non-increasing. Hence, if vik<θv^k_i < \thetavik​<θ for some kkk, then vik+j<θv^{k+j}_i < \thetavik+j​<θ for all j⩾0j \geq 0j⩾0.

Figure 5.1 illustrates a growing wave of failures that can arise in a financial network. Firms with lighter colors have better balance sheets. Black firms have failed. The code for generating this figure, along with details on parameters, can be found in the code book.

5.3Chapter Notes¶

Shin (2010) gives an excellent overview of systemic risk and the financial crisis of 2007–2008. Battiston et al. (2012) study connectedness in financial networks and introduce a measure of systemic impact called DebtRank. Bardoscia et al. (2015) provide a dynamic theory of instability related to DebtRank. Demange (2018) provides a threat index for contagion in financial networks related to Katz centrality. Bardoscia et al. (2019) analyze risks associated with solvency contagion during crises. Jackson & Pernoud (2019) study investment in risky portfolios by banks in financial networks with debt and equity interdependencies. Jackson & Pernoud (2020) analyze optimal bailouts in financial networks. Amini & Minca (2020) offer an introduction to modeling of clearing systems, analyzing equilibria for network payments and asset prices. Jackson & Pernoud (2021) provide a survey of the relationship between financial networks and systemic risk.

The setting in Section 5.2.2.3 was investigated by Eisenberg & Noe (2001), one of the first papers on a network approach to default cascades. Additional details on stability properties can be found in Stachurski (2022). As already mentioned, Section 5.2.3 is based on Elliott et al., 2014, which also includes an interesting discussion of how the level of integration across a network affects equilibria. Klages-Mundt & Minca (2021) discuss optimal intervention in economic networks via influence maximization methods, using Elliott et al. (2014) as an example. Acemoglu et al. (2021) study how anticipation of future defaults can result in "credit freezes."

A general discussion of contraction maps and related fixed point theory can be found in Goebel & Kirk (1990) and Cheney (2013). For more on fixed point methods for order preserving operators, see, for example, Guo et al. (2004), Zhang (2012), Marinacci & Montrucchio (2019) or Deplano et al. (2020).
